Lampstand
LAMP-stand
noun (biblical theology / tabernacle furnishings / typology)
Hebrew menorah (“lampstand, candelabrum”), from the root nor (lamp) or 'or (light); English “lampstand” translates Hebrew menorah and Greek lychnia (λυχνíα); the tabernacle lampstand (Exod 25:31–40; 37:17–24) was the single most visually elaborate piece of tabernacle furniture: hammered from a single talent (approximately 75 lbs) of pure gold, with a central shaft and six branches bearing seven lamps, decorated with almond-blossom ornaments; it stood in the Holy Place and provided the only artificial light inside the tabernacle

See also: Lampstand

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The lampstand is the golden seven-branched candelabrum that stood on the south side of the Holy Place in the tabernacle (and later in Solomon's temple, which had ten lampstands) and provided continuous light to the priestly service. Its function was practical — the only light in the enclosed Holy Place — but its primary significance is theological and typological. It burned continually (Lev 24:2: “to keep a lamp burning continually”), symbolizing the uninterrupted divine presence and witness. Aaron's command (Num 8:2–3) to arrange the seven lamps so they illumined the area in front of the lampstand directed the light forward, toward the table of showbread — God's light illuminating God's provision. Zechariah's vision (Zech 4:1–6) transforms the menorah into an image of the Spirit's inexhaustible supply: the lampstand feeds from a golden bowl of oil supplied by two olive trees without human intervention — “Not by might, nor by power, but by My Spirit” (Zech 4:6). Revelation's opening vision identifies the seven golden lampstands as the seven churches (Rev 1:20), placing the churches in the typological position of the tabernacle lampstand: they are the light of the world (Matt 5:14), sustained by the Spirit, bearing witness in the darkness. Christ walking among the lampstands (Rev 2:1) is the great High Priest tending the lamps — trimming, refilling, and if necessary removing the lampstand from its place (Rev 2:5).

Webster 1828 Definition

LAMPSTAND (MENORAH): the seven-branched golden candelabrum of the tabernacle's Holy Place (Exod 25:31–40); it burned continually (Lev 24:2); in Zechariah 4, a symbol of the Spirit's inexhaustible supply; in Revelation 1:20, the symbol of the churches as the light-bearers in the world, with Christ as the great High Priest who tends them.

LAMPSTAND. n. [Heb. menorah, from 'or, light.] The seven-branched golden candelabrum of the tabernacle's Holy Place; commanded in Exodus 25:31–40 and constructed in 37:17–24; a single talent of pure gold hammered (miqshah, beaten work) into a central shaft with six branches, three on each side, each branch terminating in a lamp-bowl shaped like an almond blossom.

Physical specifications: seven lamps in total, fed with pure olive oil (Exod 27:20); trimmed morning and evening by Aaron (Exod 30:7–8); positioned on the south side of the Holy Place, directly opposite the table of showbread on the north; its light was the only continuous interior light in the enclosed tabernacle, making it the visual center of the priestly service space.

Zechariah's vision (Zech 4:1–14): the prophet sees a golden lampstand with a bowl on top connected to two olive trees, supplying oil continuously without human intervention. The divine interpretation: “Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit” (4:6) — the lampstand's light is Spirit-sustained, not human-maintained. The vision concerned the rebuilding of the temple by Zerubbabel and the Messianic implications of that work.

Revelation's churches as lampstands (Rev 1:12–20): John sees seven golden lampstands with Christ walking among them; 1:20 identifies them as the seven churches. The imagery is deliberate: the churches are the new Holy Place, bearing the light of Christ in the world; Christ is the high priest attending to the lamps; a church that loses its witness is threatened with removal of its lampstand (Rev 2:5).

Temple lampstands: Solomon's temple had ten golden lampstands, five on each side of the Holy Place (1 Kings 7:49). The menorah motif persists in Zechariah's restored temple imagery and in the New Testament churches as the eschatological temple community.

Key Scripture

Exod 25:31 — "“You shall also make a lampstand of pure gold; the lampstand shall be of hammered work. Its shaft, its branches, its bowls, its ornamental knobs, and flowers shall be of one piece."

Num 8:2 — "Speak to Aaron and say to him, When you set up the lamps, the seven lamps shall give light in front of the lampstand."

Zech 4:2 — "And he said to me, “What do you see?” So I said, “I am looking, and there is a lampstand of solid gold with a bowl on top of it, and on the stand seven lamps with seven pipes to the seven lamps."

Rev 1:20 — "As for the mystery of the seven stars you saw in My right hand, and of the seven golden lampstands: the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches, and the seven lampstands are the seven churches.""

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The recovery principle is the typological chain: from the tabernacle lampstand through Zechariah's Spirit-sustained vision through Revelation's churches-as-lampstands — the church's witness is Christ's light, not its own, Spirit-sustained and Christ-tended.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The recovery principle is typological continuity. The lampstand appears at three critical moments in the biblical-theological arc: as the Holy Place light in the tabernacle/temple pointing to divine presence; as Zechariah's vision of the Spirit-sustained witness of the restored community; and as Revelation's image of the churches in the world. The thread connecting all three is that the light is not self-generated: the tabernacle lamp burned on pure olive oil poured by human hands; Zechariah's lamp was fed by the Spirit without human work; Revelation's churches walk in the light of the One who is the Light of the world (John 8:12). The church that loses its lampstand status has not merely lost a ministry program; it has been removed from the place of Spirit-sustained witness.

A pastoral misapplication to guard against: the use of Revelation 2:5 (“I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place”) as a threat of physical church closure rather than as a warning of the loss of genuine Gospel witness. The removal of the lampstand means the loss of the community's function as a light-bearer, not necessarily the closure of its building or the dissolution of its membership rolls. A church can be institutionally present and spiritually a lampstand-less husk. Conversely, a faithful remnant in a shuttered building may still be burning. The metaphor concerns faithfulness and witness, not institutional survival.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew menorah (lampstand) from root 'or (light); the tabernacle's single talent of hammered pure gold; its continuous burning as the visible sign of divine presence and witness; Spirit-sustained in Zechariah; churches-as-lampstands in Revelation; the chain from Exodus through Zechariah to Revelation as the typological arc of Christ as light of the world.

expand to see more

Hebrew menorah — lampstand, candelabrum; the specific word for this piece of sacred furniture; modern Judaism's identification of the menorah as the symbol of Israel's existence and mission is rooted in this tabernacle origin and in the Maccabean miracle (Hanukkah) of the temple's re-dedication, when the lampstand burned eight days on one day's oil

Miqshah (hammered work, Exod 25:31) — the lampstand was beaten from a single piece of gold, not assembled from separate parts; this structural unity (one shaft, one body, all branches from the same source) may typologically suggest the unity of the light-bearing community: the church does not produce its own light from separate sources but receives it from the one source

Pure olive oil (Exod 27:20; Lev 24:2) — the fuel for the lampstand was specifically pure pressed olive oil; in Scripture, oil is the consistent symbol of the Holy Spirit's anointing (Ps 45:7; Isa 61:1; Acts 10:38); the lampstand's dependence on oil to give light prefigures the church's dependence on the Spirit to bear witness

Aaron's daily trimming (Exod 30:7–8) — the lamps were attended morning and evening by the high priest; in Revelation's typological reading, Christ walking among the lampstands (Rev 2:1) is the eschatological fulfillment: He trims, refills, and attends to each lamp, removing dross and restoring flame; the pastoral care of the churches belongs to Him

Zechariah 4 and the Spirit without measure — the vision of the lampstand fed by two olive trees without human intermediary work becomes the scriptural ground for understanding the Spirit's sufficiency: the light that witnesses does not depend on human capacity, fundraising, or programmatic effort; “Not by might, nor by power, but by My Spirit” (4:6) is the theological summary of the lampstand's fuel-source

Usage

"The lampstand typology provides a powerful framework for preaching Revelation 2–3 (the seven letters to the churches). Each letter is addressed to a church that is a lampstand: a light-bearing community in the darkness of Asia Minor's pagan cities. The threats, encouragements, and warnings of each letter are addressed to communities whose primary calling is to burn — to bear Christ's light through faithfulness to His word, worship, and moral integrity. The lampstand-removal threat (Rev 2:5, to Ephesus) makes the mission clear: losing first love is not a minor spiritual problem; it is the loss of the community's reason for existence as a light-bearer."

"The Spirit-sustained character of the lampstand (Zech 4:6: “Not by might, nor by power, but by My Spirit”) is the antidote to programmatic exhaustion in ministry. Churches that substitute institutional programming for Spirit-sustained witness discover that the lamps go dark even as the activity intensifies. The lampstand burned when the Spirit supplied the oil; it was trimmed by the high priest's daily attention. Both elements are present in the healthy church: Spirit-dependence and Christ-centered Word ministry."

"The seven lampstands as the seven churches (Rev 1:20) ground a theology of the local church as the primary form of Christ's visible presence in the world. The lampstand does not burn abstractly; it burns in a specific location, among specific people, in a specific historical moment. The church at Ephesus burned in Ephesus; the church at Smyrna in Smyrna. The Reformed tradition's emphasis on the local church as the primary expression of the kingdom is supported by this imagery: the light is local before it is global, embodied before it is institutional, gathered before it is scattered."
